articles.title: Türkiye slams latest Houthi attack on Saudi capital Riyadh
articles.summary: Türkiye on Sunday condemned "in the strongest terms" the latest Houthi attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh, according to the Foreign...
articles.full_text:
Türkiye on Sunday condemned "in the strongest terms" the latest Houthi attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh, according to the Foreign Ministry.
"We condemn in the strongest terms the Houthi targeting of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, once again," the ministry said in a statement.
Ankara expressed condolences to the families of those killed in the attack and wished a speedy recovery to the injured, while conveying its sympathies to the Saudi people.
"We wish Allah’s mercy upon those who lost their lives in the attacks and a speedy recovery to the injured," it added.
The ministry said attacks deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and innocent civilians constitute clear violations of international law and the principles of international humanitarian law.
"These attacks, which target civilians and civilian infrastructure and further escalate tensions in the region, must cease immediately."
It also slammed actions that threaten regional security and stability while undermining the international community's joint efforts to establish peace.
"We reaffirm our full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reiterate our call for the resolution of ongoing conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy," it added.

articles.title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia raise risk of wider war - The Business Times
articles.summary: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia raise risk of wider war  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
With an American among those killed, US president Donald Trump faces growing pressure to act
THIS weekend’s deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport have demonstrated the ability of Yemen’s Houthis to strike at the heart of Saudi power, raising the risk of a dangerous escalation that could draw in the US.
Saturday’s strike killed 12 people and wounded 309, while on Sunday (Oct 11) the airport was hit again, this time by an unknown projectile, the fourth attack in a week.
Saudi fighter jets are already backing a counter-offensive by Yemeni government forces after the Houthis seized territory near Bab el-Mandeb, a critical chokepoint for global shipping at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis had largely stayed on the sidelines after the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February.
But the latest offensive illustrates how the group – a member of Iran’s so-called axis of resistance – has developed into its own autonomous fighting force, with its own sophisticated weapons supply chain and an ability to operate and escalate as they see fit, at times in coordination with the Islamic Republic.
The attacks put de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman under mounting pressure to escalate a war the country has spent years trying to escape, against an opponent that is arguably more capable than it has ever been.
They also present difficult choices for the US and the kingdom’s new defence partners, Turkey and Pakistan, over how far to go in helping Saudi Arabia respond.
“By escalating their attacks, they are trying to pressure Saudi Arabia into stepping back and halting its air campaign,” said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen.
“Riyadh sees these strikes as a serious escalation, particularly given their unprecedented nature, and is likely to respond with greater military pressure.”
The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s attack, calling it “a full-fledged war crime”.
The group has not claimed responsibility for that strike, although it claimed earlier attacks and has warned of further strikes on Saudi airports.
Saudi Arabia led a coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to restore the internationally recognised government, only to spend years bombing the Houthis without dislodging them.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced the fighting and offered Riyadh a way to wind down its involvement while the militant group’s capabilities and reach grew.
Saudi Arabia has spent billions of dollars building one of the region’s most sophisticated militaries, equipped with American F-15 fighter jets and Patriot missile defences whose interceptors cost as much as US$5 million apiece.
Yet repeated strikes have shuttered the international airport serving its capital, grounding hundreds of flights and forcing schools to move online.
The attacks may be a sign of the pressure the Houthis are facing in Yemen.
After the group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and territory near Bab el-Mandeb last month, Yemeni government forces launched a counter-offensive backed by Saudi warplanes.
The coalition says it has recaptured Mokha and destroyed scores of Houthi military targets.
“The Houthis are feeling the impact of the Saudi airstrikes carried out over the past few days in areas under their control,” Nagi said.
“They have lost a significant number of fighters, and several strategic sites have been hit, including drone workshops, arms depots and telecommunications towers.”
Still, the Houthis retain an arsenal of Iranian-designed ballistic missiles capable of reaching Riyadh and cheap attack drones that can be assembled locally.
The group has survived years of Saudi and US bombing campaigns, and the latest strikes demonstrate how difficult it may be to stop it from inflicting further damage on the kingdom.
“They appear to have enough cheap drones and missiles, as well as the know-how, to conduct long-range strikes against Saudi civilian infrastructure, which is a soft target,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security think tank who previously worked in strategy at the Pentagon.
The attacks also present difficult choices for Saudi Arabia’s allies, starting with the US, which launched major strikes against the Houthis last year before agreeing to a truce.
US President Donald Trump has sought to avoid further military escalation with Iran ahead of November’s midterm elections, and Washington has so far limited its support for the Saudi offensive to intelligence sharing.
“It is very unlikely that the Saudis can stop the attacks if the US could not – short of sending in ground forces or dramatically improving the capability of the Yemeni fighters it is supporting,” Pettyjohn said.
“Suppression requires constant air patrols searching for launchers, which is difficult. And the Yemenis seem to have used the time since the ceasefire with the US to rearm.”
But with an American among those killed on Saturday, Trump faces growing pressure to act.
Asked on Saturday whether the US would join strikes against the Houthis, he said: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”
“Riyadh will want direct US strikes against the Houthis, air defence capabilities, increased intelligence sharing, and political cover for an intensified campaign in Yemen,” said William Usher, a former senior Middle East analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency.
Riyadh has grown frustrated with the limited assistance from its Western allies, according to people familiar with the matter.
Britain has provided an air-refuelling aircraft, but Saudi requests for additional defensive support in recent weeks have yet to be approved, said the people, requesting anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
France said it will dispatch defensive military equipment to the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The escalation also poses a test for Turkey and Pakistan, which signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia in August, known as the Mecca Defense Alliance.
Both have signalled willingness to send troops or weapons to help defend the kingdom, but Turkey has ruled out joining offensive operations against the Houthis.
For Saudi Arabia, the Houthis’ success comes at a challenging time.
The kingdom is set to host a series of events aimed at pitching itself as one of the world’s most lucrative investment plays.
That includes its flagship Future Investment Initiative, often dubbed Davos in the Desert, which draws Wall Street titans from Goldman Sachs’ David Solomon to BlackRock’s Larry Fink.
Executives at top oil firms including BP and Shell pulled out of the World Petroleum Congress scheduled to start on Sunday, in a sign of how the attacks are already disrupting business in Riyadh.
The capital’s financial district, home to the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund and major foreign banks and consultancies, also shifted to remote work.
The attacks come as the Middle East’s largest economy faces growing financial strain after years of heavy spending on the crown prince’s Vision 2030 transformation agenda.
The government this month increased its budget deficit projection and said the economy will probably contract 3.6 per cent this year, making foreign investment and financing even more critical.
“The latest events may be a disruption to foreign investment but investors and partners won’t be pulling out. They will be observing and waiting to get in,” said Said El-Saadi, chief executive of Access KSA, a Saudi-based international business advisory firm.
Still, Saudi leaders may conclude they have little choice but to escalate if they want to end the attacks and restore peace.
“The Houthis have always been aggressive and willing to take risks,” said Nadwa Al-Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute.
“They only back down when faced with a credible threat, and so far, they haven’t faced one.” BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days - BBC
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days  BBC
articles.full_text:
- Published
One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said.
A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack.
It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.
The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.
The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.
They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.
On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.
US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.
Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".
Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".
The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. A residential home in the city was also struck, killing a child and injuring six people, the media outlet reported.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attacks and the BBC has been unable to verify this report.
Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners.
Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals. The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport.
There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that.
The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions.
The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control.
Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi Arabian counterpart on Sunday that his country was ready to provide assistance to "facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen", referring to the Houthi administration.

articles.title: Iran sets supertanker ablaze after US takes out ship breaking blockade - New York Post
articles.summary: Iran sets supertanker ablaze after US takes out ship breaking blockade  New York PostAfter oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping  CNNTanker attacks in Strait of Hormuz surge to wartime high as Iran tries to choke off oil exports  CNBCHormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall  Al JazeeraVessel struck by unknown projectile off UAE coast amid surge in attacks, UKMTO says  Reuters
articles.full_text:
A supertanker caught fire when it was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, officials said — just hours after the US struck a ship attempting to break its naval blockade on Iran.
The attacked supertanker, which was not immediately identified, was hit on its port side, causing a fire to break out, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations.
The IRGC shared video of the tanker ablaze in the water as it reiterated its threats on any ship attempting to cross the strait without its permission.
“A devastating fire is the fate of any tanker that violates the rules and disregards security in the Strait of Hormuz,” the military unit said in a statement.
At least 11 tankers have come under attack during the week that ended Oct. 4, the most strikes on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began Feb. 28, according to the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization.
Another 10 strikes occurred last week, including one Monday that left 12 Indian sailors injured aboard the United Arab Emirates-owned On Peace oil tanker.
The latest attack came just hours after US Central Command confirmed that it took out a commercial cargo ship attempting to run the US’s naval blockade against Iran.
“A US military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew,” CENTCOM wrote in a statement.
The ship had allegedly docked at an Iranian port and was attempting to leave the region for international waters, CENTCOM added.
US forces have disabled four ships and turned around another 135 since it renewed its naval blockade three months ago.

articles.title: Deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport draws int'l condemnation
articles.summary: The international community joined in unison Sunday to condemn the deadly Houthi attack on Saudi capital Riyadh. U.N. and EU leaders voiced shock at the attack and warned against a...
articles.full_text:
The international community joined in unison Sunday to condemn the deadly Houthi attack on Saudi capital Riyadh.
U.N. and EU leaders voiced shock at the attack and warned against an escalation in the deadly conflict.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by Saturday's attack on Riyadh's airport, which killed 12 people and wounded over 300, according to aviation authorities.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," Guterres said in a statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that Washington may join Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen following the attack.
Asked by reporters whether he had decided to take part in the strikes, Trump said: "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack. We will make a decision. We move very quickly."
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called the attack a "dangerous escalation" and said the Iran-backed group must halt strikes on civilian targets.
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
"These murderous attacks at civilians must stop at once," she said, adding the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia."
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he "firmly condemns" the attack, which he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation."
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, U.K. Defense Minister Wes Streeting said the attacks were "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation"
France also condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
France, which is already lending troops and military equipment to Saudi Arabia, "will continue to remain by its side in its defense of its territory and its infrastructure," a Foreign Ministry statement said, calling on the Houthis to cease their attacks.
Meanwhile, Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif strongly condemned the deadly attack on Saudi capital's international airport.
"Attacks targeting civilians and vital infrastructure are utterly unacceptable and pose a serious threat to regional peace and stability," Sharif posted on X, describing the attack as "heinous" and reaffirming Pakistan's "steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, territorial integrity."
Pakistan is close ally of Saudi Arabia and are part of the Mecca mutual defense pact alongside Türkiye.
Another Saudi ally, Syria also condemned "in the strongest terms" Saturday's deadly attack on King Khalid International Airport.
It stressed that the security of Saudi Arabia is an "integral part of the security of Syria and the entire region."
In a statement released on X, the Syrian Foreign Ministry described the attack as "a violation of the Kingdom's sovereignty and a direct threat to its security and stability, as well as to the safety of civilians, civilian facilities, and air navigation."
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim "unequivocally denounced" the attack, saying "there can be no justification for attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure."
Anwar said on X that putting innocent lives at risk "can only deepen the suffering already wrought by this conflict and carry it into places that should remain beyond its reach."
He also said Malaysia stands in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its people "at this perilous hour," and that Kuala Lumpur remains "steadfast in our hope that diplomacy and reason will prevail before the conflict widens still further."
Bangladesh also "strongly and unequivocally" condemned the attack in an official statement. Two Bangladeshi nationals have been killed in the strike.
"Attacks endangering civilian lives and targeting civilian infrastructure are unacceptable and must cease immediately," the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said.
The Muslim-majority South Asian nation also called for an "immediate cessation of hostilities, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and a peaceful resolution of the ongoing crisis through dialogue and diplomacy, in the interest of regional peace, security and stability."
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia on Sunday kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online as Yemen's Houthi rebels threatened new airstrikes across the kingdom.
Saturday's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran's-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

articles.title: Saudi coalition fumes after Houthi strike kills 12 at Riyadh airport
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unraveled in July.
The spiraling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with U.S. President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger said they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one U.S. citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation," a medical source said.
Two doctors told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday, citing an order from the education ministry, saying "all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week".
"The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia ... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime," coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes Saturday.
Saturday's attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Daesh terrorist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shiite mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, U.N.-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbor's conflict.
Asked Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: "We may."
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom "not acceptable."
U.S. media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for U.S. military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week."
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack" and reaffirmed Islamabad's commitment to Saudi Arabia's security under their defense pact.
The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counteroffensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key choke point for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia and the New Strategic Balance in the Middle East - Tirana Times
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and the New Strategic Balance in the Middle East  Tirana Times
articles.full_text:
The Middle East faces a historic choice: to remain trapped in rivalries that define security through the weakening of adversaries, or to build a regional order based on sovereignty, cooperation and diplomacy.
By Dr. Arben Ramkaj
Tirana Times, October 11, 2026 – The greatest danger facing the Middle East today is not merely the outbreak of another war, but the possibility that existing conflicts could converge into an uncontrollable regional confrontation. The October 10 attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which left 12 people dead and 309 injured, according to Saudi authorities, has brought this danger sharply into focus. For Saudi Arabia, the custodian of Islam’s two holiest sites in Mecca and Medina, the challenge is to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens without allowing military escalation to determine the region’s future.
The magnitude of this challenge becomes clearer against the backdrop of the upheavals that have transformed the Middle East. The Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli military offensive in Gaza have resulted in tens of thousands of civilian casualties and a humanitarian catastrophe that has shocked international public opinion. Millions of people have taken to the streets around the world, demanding an end to the war and the Israeli offensive. The destruction of civilian infrastructure and the deteriorating situation in the West Bank have turned the conflict into a question of international conscience and responsibility.
In this atmosphere, Pope Francis’s warning about a “Third World War fought piecemeal” resonates with particular urgency. The war in Ukraine and the crises unfolding across the Middle East have created a reality in which conflicts increasingly influence and reinforce one another. Unlike the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the danger was concentrated in a single confrontation, today’s risks are dispersed across multiple fronts that could ultimately converge.
At the heart of this uncertainty lies the rivalry between Iran and Israel, accompanied by strategic ambitions, not always openly articulated, to expand influence and establish political and military dominance in the Middle East. Tehran has projected influence through Hezbollah in Lebanon, armed groups in Iraq and the Houthi movement in Yemen, while Israel relies on its military superiority and operations beyond its borders. Syria has demonstrated the human and political cost of these rivalries, where Iranian support for Bashar al-Assad’s regime contributed to prolonging the civil war. The confrontation between these two powers risks holding the region hostage to competing ambitions for hegemony.
It is precisely within this complex strategic environment that Saudi Arabia’s positioning has acquired particular significance.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close partner of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, has repeatedly encouraged the Kingdom to normalize relations with Israel and join the Abraham Accords. Against the backdrop of the rivalry with Iran, such a step would strengthen regional security cooperation. Yet, despite expectations among international policymakers and analysts, the Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister has prioritized a principle closely linked to the Kingdom’s historical and moral responsibilities: the establishment of an independent Palestinian state as a prerequisite for normalization with Israel.
This position has been translated into concrete diplomatic action. Together with France, Saudi Arabia spearheaded an international initiative to advance the two-state solution, helping generate renewed momentum toward recognition of Palestinian statehood. In September 2025, France, the United Kingdom and several other European countries took this historic step. Although their decisions also reflected domestic political considerations, Saudi diplomacy contributed to creating a new international dynamic.
But could this principled position itself be part of the strategic price Saudi Arabia is paying today? The question demands caution. Future developments will determine whether Riyadh’s insistence on Palestinian statehood becomes a foundation for lasting regional stability or exposes the Kingdom to new pressures.
Within this framework, Riyadh seeks to move the Palestinian question away from military confrontation and toward international legitimacy. Unlike Iran’s approach, in which support for Palestine has been intertwined with the activities of armed groups, Saudi Arabia advocates a diplomatic settlement based on the two-state solution.
Such an approach requires strengthening the Palestinian Authority, led by President Mahmoud Abbas, and renewing its democratic legitimacy. The parliamentary and presidential elections announced for 2027 could contribute to institutional consolidation and the political reunification of Gaza and the West Bank.
At the same time, Riyadh is broadening its strategic partnerships. Discussions about closer cooperation with Turkey and Pakistan are particularly significant given their respective strategic positions: Turkey is a NATO member, while Pakistan is a nuclear power with extensive diplomatic relationships. Such cooperation could strengthen consultation mechanisms and crisis prevention, provided that it does not create new regional dividing lines.
While these partnerships are intended to reinforce future security, Yemen remains a critical test of the existing regional balance.
The Saudi-led coalition’s military intervention in March 2015 followed a request from Yemen’s internationally recognized president, Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi, after the advance of Houthi forces. United Nations Security Council Resolution 2216, adopted on April 14, 2015, demanded that the Houthis withdraw from territories they had seized and surrender weapons taken from state institutions. The resolution remains an important international reference concerning Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Nevertheless, the Yemeni experience demonstrates that security cannot be achieved through military means alone. Riyadh has supported United Nations mediation and political dialogue, while Houthi attacks against international shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Saudi civilian infrastructure continue to threaten regional stability. Any response must respect international law and the protection of civilians.
The humanitarian dimension is equally important. Saudi Arabia has reported providing more than $20 billion in overall support to Yemen, encompassing humanitarian assistance, economic support and development projects. Yet without institutional reconstruction and domestic reconciliation, the country’s recovery will remain fragile.
The consequences of the crisis extend far beyond the Arabian Peninsula. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal form vital commercial corridors connecting Asia and Europe. Attacks on merchant vessels have transformed maritime security into a matter of multilateral responsibility, making diplomacy, international cooperation and respect for international law indispensable.
In this environment, where stability increasingly depends on international cooperation, Albania also has an opportunity to assume responsibilities beyond its immediate neighborhood.
As a NATO member and a participant in the Board of Peace for Gaza, Albania should consider contributing to the logistical component of a Saudi-led multilateral initiative within formally established international mechanisms. Such an engagement would be a meaningful contribution by Albania, strengthening its strategic relations with Saudi Arabia and its Euro-Atlantic partners while giving Albanian foreign policy a more active role in international efforts to promote peace and regional stability.
Ultimately, the Middle East stands at a historic crossroads. It can remain trapped in rivalries that define security through the weakening of adversaries, or it can begin building a regional order founded on sovereignty, cooperation and diplomacy.
Saudi Arabia possesses the resources, influence and international relationships necessary to help shape this transformation. Yet its future strategic weight will depend not only on its ability to project power, but also on its capacity to translate that influence into international responsibility.

About the Author
Dr. Arben Ramkaj is Director of the Middle East and Arab World Program at the Albanian Institute for International Studies (AIIS), Chairman of the Interreligious Cooperation Center and Vice President of the European Muslim League.

articles.title: Israel and Saudi Arabia consider benefits, risks of regional alliance - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Israel and Saudi Arabia consider benefits, risks of regional alliance  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump lives in a transactional foreign policy universe. You give, you get. You don’t give, don’t expect much.
Israel has given a lot and, in return, gotten a lot. It has fought wing to wing with the US in Iran, provided valuable intelligence and demonstrated the military capabilities Washington wants to see in an ally.
In April, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, “To our Israeli allies, thanks for being a brave, capable and willing ally on this battlefield. The rest of the world and the rest of our so-called allies saw what real capabilities look like. They should take some notes.”
America’s “legacy” allies – from NATO countries to South Korea – have not stepped up to anywhere near the same degree. They have consequently been on the receiving end of more than just harsh words.
Trump ordered joint military exercises with South Korea scaled back, citing Seoul’s refusal to help with the Iran campaign, and threatened to cut off trade with Spain after Madrid denied Washington the use of its bases for strikes on Iran.
And then there is Saudi Arabia.
Many have been puzzled by Washington’s reluctance to intervene directly in the Saudis’ battle with the Houthis. This battle took a particularly deadly turn on Saturday when the King Khalid Airport in Riyadh was struck by a missile, killing 12 people and injuring more than 300, the most serious attack in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
This came as tensions between the Saudis and the Houthis steadily escalated – Saturday’s attack was the third such attack in a week, since the Saudis launched a counter-offensive against the Houthis to push them back from the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Despite all that, Trump has wavered. Washington has provided intelligence and targeting assistance, but the president has so far stopped short of direct military intervention. On Saturday, he said he was considering joining the Saudi strikes.
Why the hesitation?
The explanations offered range from reluctance to become engaged in another major military campaign less than a month before the midterm elections to concern about weapons stocks depleted by the war in Iran.
Saudi Arabia's refusal to join the Abraham Accords
Another possible explanation is Trump’s frustration with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s steadfast refusal to join the Abraham Accords. Saudi normalization with Israel would have given Trump an important diplomatic prize before the elections.
If this is indeed the case, then it fits into a pattern. In July, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a nuclear cooperation agreement, opening the door to a major commercial role for American companies. Trump then said he would not proceed unless the Saudis joined the Abraham Accords.
You give, you get.
Saudi normalization with Israel has long been the Middle East’s diplomatic holy grail.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, said in a long, revealing interview with Israel Hayom on Thursday that the desire to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords helped explain Israel’s restraint toward Hamas and Hezbollah in the run-up to October 7.
Israel wanted to avoid an escalation that could derail the normalization process. He said the two countries were “closer than people realize” to a deal.
But Israeli action didn’t scuttle the process. Hamas did that all on its own.
Since then, the Saudis have made clear – even as the Iranian threat loomed larger and normalization with Israel made good strategic sense in trying to create a new security architecture for the region – that without a pathway to a Palestinian state, they were not going to normalize.
That leaves a familiar gap between strategic logic and political feasibility, since – with October 7 so fresh and raw – it is highly unlikely that any Israeli government in the foreseeable future would agree to a Palestinian state.
Israel and Saudi Arabia face threats from Iran and its allies. Both have an interest in preventing the Houthis from threatening shipping, airports, and regional stability. Those shared interests provide a strong argument for cooperation. They have not, however, proven enough to overcome the political obstacles to establishing an open relationship.
Further evidence of where Riyadh was looking for its regional security architecture came in August, when it signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. Rather than bringing its relationship with Israel into the open, Saudi Arabia was strengthening an alternative framework with two Muslim powers.
The pact’s promise was sweeping: an attack on one would be considered an attack on all. So far, the response to the Houthi campaign has not matched that rhetoric. Turkey has reportedly begun providing defensive and technical assistance, but that is a long way from joining Saudi Arabia in striking the enemy attacking it.
Signing this pact showed that Saudi Arabia – while interested in maintaining intelligence cooperation with Israel and keeping it discreet – was seeking far-reaching security arrangements elsewhere.
Then an Omani pilot planned to crash a flydubai plane full of Israeli passengers into Ben-Gurion Airport, only to be thwarted by some brave and resourceful passengers and crew members, and Jerusalem got an unvarnished view of where it stands with the Saudis.
Yes, the Saudis allowed a distressed plane full of Israeli passengers to land at a civilian-military airfield in Tabuk. And, yes, Saudi medical personnel cared for Israeli passengers. Both were consequential acts of assistance in a moment of acute danger.
But Riyadh adamantly refused Israel’s request to send its own aircraft to collect the passengers. A replacement flydubai plane brought them home.
Cooperation, but to a point
This exposed the boundary between practical cooperation and public acceptance. Allowing an Israeli plane to pick up the passengers would be one gesture too far on the road to normalization: one which would have been staunchly opposed by much of the Saudi public and undoubtedly weaponized against the Saudis by the Iranians.
Whatever the precise calculations behind that refusal, the political message was clear: cooperation could proceed, but only so far.
Ten days later, Saudi Arabia’s own airport was targeted, and all of a sudden it is looking for allies in its fight with the Houthis.
That attack inevitably led to speculation that this might bring Israeli-Saudi security cooperation into the open and lead to closer ties to combat a common threat. Weakening the Houthis, after all, would serve Israeli interests as well as Saudi ones. The group’s hostility toward Israel is not exactly a secret.
But shared enemies don’t necessarily lead to joint military operations. Public Israeli involvement could carry political costs for Riyadh and provide ammunition for those seeking to portray the Saudi campaign as serving Israel.
The Saudi leadership would have to weigh those costs against the benefits of the assistance. Israel, in turn, would have to decide what risks it should take on the Saudis’ behalf and what it could expect in return.
While the airport attack does not guarantee a breakthrough between Israel and Saudi Arabia, it does force Riyadh to face this question: does it make sense to keep one of its potentially strongest regional partners at arm’s length?
And for Israel, the question is a variation on Trump’s transactional theme: How much should it give when the Saudis are still unwilling to publicly be seen taking?

articles.title: Iran may be restoring activity at nuclear-linked site struck by Israel - Iran International
articles.summary: Iran may be restoring activity at nuclear-linked site struck by Israel  Iran International
articles.full_text:
New construction and repairs at an Iranian compound previously targeted by Israel suggest Tehran may be moving beyond clearing war damage toward restoring operations at a site linked to nuclear weapons research, according to a Washington-based research institute.
The Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) said Saturday that satellite imagery showed repairs to what appeared to be a water tank and the addition of a small building nearby at the Minzadayi compound, northeast of Tehran.
The findings add to an assessment published Tuesday in which the institute identified unusually heavy vehicle traffic and earth-moving activity at the heavily secured site, which Israeli aircraft struck on March 3.
The latest observations suggest Iran is seeking “not just to clean up the site” but to resume regular activities there, the institute said in a post on X.
Iran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons, maintaining that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes.
The International Atomic Energy Agency has said it has no credible indication of a coordinated Iranian nuclear weapons program, although it has repeatedly raised concerns about Tehran's uranium enrichment and unresolved questions over past nuclear activities.
The original ISIS report, based on high-resolution satellite images taken in September and October, documented passenger vehicles and trucks returning to the compound following extensive work to remove rubble and repair damage from the Israeli attack.
Researchers also identified continued excavation at a section of the compound where the March strikes had left several craters, apparently above underground structures.
The institute said the activity could indicate an attempt to restore capabilities associated with nuclear weapons development. But the images do not establish what work, if any, has resumed inside the compound.
Israel identified Minzadayi as a covert nuclear weapons development facility during the war, saying scientists there had been working on a component of a nuclear weapons system. The institute's assessment of the site's earlier purpose relies partly on those Israeli military claims, which have not been independently verified.
The US and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28, two days after indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva that Omani mediators said had made progress. Further technical talks had been planned before the attacks began.
Washington and Tehran remain divided over the future of Iran's nuclear program. The Trump administration is demanding substantial reductions in Iran's enrichment capacity, while Tehran insists it will not surrender its right to enrich uranium.
On Saturday, the Kremlin said Russian President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's position on a possible settlement of the war to President Donald Trump during a phone call Friday, following consultations with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Moscow disclosed neither the details of Iran's position nor Trump's response.
The institute's findings raise the possibility that Iran is rebuilding infrastructure damaged in the war, but leave unanswered the more consequential question of whether any nuclear weapons-related research has resumed.

articles.title: Some Israeli settlers use sheep as tool to push Palestinians from their West Bank homes - CBS News
articles.summary: Some Israeli settlers use sheep as tool to push Palestinians from their West Bank homes  CBS News60 Minutes Transcript: The West Bank, where Israeli settler violence against Palestinians is surging  CBS NewsWith attention on Gaza and Iran, Israeli settlers grab land in West Bank  The Washington PostThree years of Israel’s mass dispossession of West Bank Palestinians  Al JazeeraOpinion | Otherwise Occupied • Settlers commit the pogroms. Israel's public enab...
articles.full_text:
The arid hilltops of the West Bank have seen shepherds come and go for thousands of years, and now some of these shepherds are behind settler violence against Palestinians.
The struggle for the West Bank is a biblical story. There are two populations – Jewish and Arab, the descendants of Abraham's sons, Isaac and Ishmael – fighting over ancestral land. The West Bank, located on the west bank of the Jordan River, is home to more than 3 million Palestinians who hope to make it the heart of their future state. It is also home to over 500,000 Jews who call the area Judea and Samaria, their biblical homeland.
The area has been under Israeli military occupation for nearly six decades. Jewish settlers have built communities in the West Bank in hopes of making the land part of Israel.
With Israeli elections two weeks away, and midterms in the U.S. next month, how settler violence is handled could soon change.
Driving sheep herds into Palestinian communities
Mordehai Minster, who cofounded a sheep farm in the West Bank, is a new type of Israeli settler. His herd is driven deeper and deeper into surrounding Palestinian communities.
"When you have sheep, everyone understands. Arabs tend to fight over grazing lands among themselves. It's a language that we understand, and they understand," Minster said. "And it's a way to delineate the border. 'This is where I graze my sheep. You don't take your sheep here. You don't plant here. You don't build here.'"
Israeli sheep farms have taken over huge swathes of land: an estimated 20% of the West Bank. Some 200 sheep farms have popped up in recent years. Settlers even push sheep into Palestinian homes.
"They enter, they open the gate of the house and take the sheep inside to eat the trees around the house," Waheed Marsouq, a Palestinian teacher in Al-Mughayyir, said.
For decades, Jewish settlers put up fences to protect themselves from the active threat of Palestinian terrorism. Now it's the Palestinians who are penning themselves in. More than 100 Palestinian communities have been displaced or erased by the settler violence and the ever-encroaching sheep.
"Whenever you have ethnic religious communities, especially in the Middle East, fighting over land and resources, that conflict sometimes gets ugly," Minster said. "The fact that violence exists doesn't change the merit of the right that we have to this land."
Who are the Israeli settlers?
Young shepherds, known as Hilltop Youth, are often behind the violence. They've flocked to the West Bank for a sense of adventure, and are told they're on a God-given mission to redeem the land. They storm Palestinian fields and villages, cut down olive trees, torch cars and destroy property, and harass farmers and livestock. There have been more than 1,600 incidents so far this year, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
There's a hardcore group of up to 500 settlers, and up to 1,000 more people drift in and out.
"Those are kids that are ranging in age between, I don't know, 15 and 25," Minster said. "They don't do great in school. They don't get into the army that easily because maybe behavioral problems. So some of them end up in places like this, taking care of sheep, doing construction. Some of these kids may have drug problems. They smoke pot. They grow pot."
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has , describing it as thuggish and disgusting.
"I wouldn't classify it as terrorism, but are there some children who overreact and act in thuggish ways and need to be controlled and held in? Yeah, definitely," Minster said.
Palestinians have been .
"Yes," Minster acknowledged. "None of this is great and none of this changes the fact that our right to be here is legal and it's ancient."
"This is my land"
That is not how the Palestinians who live directly down the hill from Minster's farm see it.
Mahmoud Faraj's family has had the deed to this land for generations. 60 Minutes talked to him and his cousin Hassan about their village called Jannatah, which means paradise in Arabic.
The name was accurate until a group of 20 to 25 settlers showed up on March 26, entering the Faraj family's land and setting up a "tent," Hassan said.
"And they started to behave that they are the owners of everything," Hassan said.
The Hilltop Youth outpost, which Hassan described as a "tent," is in his backyard, cutting off access to one of their family's houses.
"This is my cousin's house over there. He's not allowed to go there at all," Mahmoud said.
The Israeli settlers are trying to force the villagers to leave, and they're succeeding, Hassan said. Many homes have been abandoned.
"They steal electricity from the locals and they also steal water," Hassan said of the settlers. "This is their strategy, to make the area unlivable."
Every time the family tries to get near their house, they say teens from the outpost rush down to beat them up. In March, Hassan tried with his uncle and cousin Muhammad.
"They started to attack us in small groups with wood sticks and with stones. And they have tear gas. And three of them, they were armed. So one of the armed guys, he started to shoot. He shot my cousin in his head," Hassan said. "And it didn't stop here. They came and they started to beat my uncle and his son, who was dead, with wood, with wood sticks."
The family is skeptical that anyone will be held responsible as only a tiny number of these cases ever get prosecuted.
On another day, Muhammad's brother, also named Hassan, tried to take 60 Minutes to the family's house. But within seconds, the Hilltop Youth in their black hoodies came running down the hill. Soon the teens were blocking Hassan from reaching the house in the distance. The teens shoved Hassan, who kept his hands behind his back so they couldn't accuse him of hitting them.
"This is my land and you won't stay. These are my roots," Hassan shouted back in Hebrew.
He was hit again and his nose was broken. One of the Hilltop Youth headbutted Hassan.
Hassan tried to retreat, but he was blocked.
Israeli activists protecting Palestinians from settlers
Hassan wasn't alone that day when he tried to visit his home. He was joined by a group of Jewish activists, called Sons of Abraham, who work to protect Palestinians under siege. They stepped between Hassan and the teenage settlers, acting as human shields. The idea is that the settlers would be more hesitant to attack other Jews.
"They are trying to push us back. They don't want us to enter with the cameras. So they are pushing and waiting for someone to react with their hands, so they have an excuse for more extreme violence," Roie, one of the activists, said.
Most of the activists, like the settlers, grew up in right-wing, religious homes. One of them, Amana, used to be a Hilltop Youth herself. But Amana, Dvir and Roie say Judaism calls on them to protect, not expel, their neighbors.
Some of the Hilltop Youth get angry when they see the Sons of Abraham.
"I think they are angrier because we threaten them ideologically," Amana said in Hebrew. "And also, I'm not coming from the outside. I also grew up as a settler. I tell them, 'I changed my ways. I know what you're doing and I know it's not the right way.'"
Sometimes the Sons of Abraham and Hilltop Youth recognize each other.
"I think it's painful for me to see how people I grew up with, and some of them were good friends of mine, behave," Roie said, acknowledging that they must say the same thing about him.
On the day Roie, Amana and Dvir accompanied Hassan, just as things were getting out of hand, a captain in the Israeli army turned up with soldiers.
In the end, Hassan was kicked off his own property. The Jewish settlers got to stay.
The army's priority is the settlers, and some soldiers are settlers themselves, and occasionally join the violence.
Though there have also been cases where the soldiers have been attacked by the young settlers.
"People call it 'settler violence.' I don't agree with that," Roie said. "It is state violence. There is a violence of a government."
Political landscape in Israel and in the U.S.
Elections in Israel are two weeks away and, so far, the Israeli government has shown an unwillingness to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank.
The has called on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to deal with the situation. Netanyahu has condemned the violence, but poured tens of millions of dollars into expanding sheep farms, arming them and giving them American-made off-roaders.
Midterm elections in the U.S. next month could also change the political landscape. If the Democrats win, they're threatening to limit military aid to Israel in part, they say, because of the West Bank attacks.
Minster said he worries about American public opinion. While he's concerned about the potential impact if Israel loses America's support, he doesn't look at it as an existential threat.
"I am bothered by the fact that America's turning on us, and we're turning on America. It's, like, I see it as losing a friendship," he said. "And I'm also concerned that, as a military ally, as a political ally, we may lose America as well. It looks like it's going in that direction. But Israel will find other allies."

articles.title: Who Are The Houthis?: The Rise Of A Militant Movement Shaping Middle East Conflict - Religion Unplugged
articles.summary: Who Are The Houthis?: The Rise Of A Militant Movement Shaping Middle East Conflict  Religion Unplugged
articles.full_text:
The Houthis, a powerful armed group based in Yemen, have emerged as one of the most influential and deadliest forces in the Middle East. Known formally as Ansar Allah, meaning “Supporters of God,” the group began as a religious and political movement in northern Yemen before developing into a military organization.
The group currently controls Yemen’s capital Sanaa and large portions of the country, challenging the internationally recognized government and confronting regional powers, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The group’s origins lie in the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam, a religious tradition historically rooted in northern Yemen. Although the movement had originally focused on protecting Zaydi identity and opposing what it viewed as political and religious marginalization, its ambitions expanded as Yemen descended into conflict.
In 2014, Houthi fighters seized Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention a year later to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The ensuing war devastated the country, contributing to widespread displacement, hunger and a humanitarian crisis.
Over the years, the Houthis have acquired stronger weapons and strengthened their military capabilities, with substantial support from nearby Iran. They have launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea and attacked Israel during the wider Mideast conflict. These operations have threatened civilian populations, international trade and regional stability.
Understanding who the Houthis are requires examining their religious roots, political objectives, regional alliances and record of violence. Their actions raise difficult questions about terrorism, national sovereignty and the protection of civilians in an already very volatile region.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis are an armed political and religious movement originating in northern Yemen. Their official name is Ansar Allah — or “Supporters of God” — and takes its popular name from the Houthi family, whose members played a leading role in its development.
The group emerged in the 1990s as a movement seeking to revive Zaydi religious traditions and challenge what its supporters considered political discrimination against northern Yemeni communities. It gradually became more militant, fighting Yemen’s government before capturing the capital more than a decade ago.
What religion are the Houthis?
The Houthis follow Zaydi Islam, a branch of Shia Islam practiced primarily in northern Yemen. Zaydism differs in important theological and historical respects from Twelver Shia Islam, the dominant form of Shiism in Iran.
Zaydi communities have a long history in Yemen, where Zaydi imams ruled parts of the country for centuries before the monarchy was overthrown in 1962. The Houthi movement draws on this religious heritage as a central element of its identity.
What do the Houthis believe?
The Houthis combine religious conservative beliefs, Yemeni nationalism, opposition to foreign intervention and hostility toward the U.S., Israel and its allies. They argue that their movement defends Yemen against foreign domination and challenges what they regard as unjust regional political arrangements.
The Houthis also oppose Saudi influence in Yemen and have portrayed the kingdom’s military operations as aggression against their country. Their leaders present their regional military campaigns as acts of resistance, including their attacks on Israel and shipping following the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023.
Why did they attack Saudi Arabia?
This past Saturday, a missile strike hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh Saudi authorities reported that at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured. The attack was part of a broader escalation in the conflict between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. Saudi Arabia blamed the Houthis for the strike. The Houthis claimed responsibility for that attack on Oct. 11.
The wider context provides some explanation. Fighting had intensified following the collapse of a ceasefire that had largely reduced hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since 2022. Saudi Arabia has resumed military operations in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, while Houthi forces have stepped up attacks against Saudi targets.
Are the Houthis a terrorist group?
Yes. The United States officially designates the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization. The U.S. government restored this designation in March 2025, following an earlier designation of the group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist entity in February 2024.
These classifications impose significant restrictions and sanctions intended to limit the group's resources and support networks. The designation also reflects concerns about the Houthis’ attacks on civilians, international shipping and regional infrastructure, as well as their threats against the United States and its allies.
The United Nations Security Council has also documented Houthi conduct involving attacks on civilian infrastructure, recruitment and use of children and obstruction of humanitarian assistance. The group has additionally been linked to repeated cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Clemente Lisi serves as executive editor at Religion Unplugged.

articles.title: Western leaders slam Houthi attack on Riyadh airport, warn citizens to stay away - RFI
articles.summary: Western leaders slam Houthi attack on Riyadh airport, warn citizens to stay away  RFI
articles.full_text:
UN and EU leaders voiced shock and anger on Sunday following an attack by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia and warned against an escalation in the deadly conflict. Several embassies have issued warnings to their citizens to avoid the area.
Issued on: Modified:
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by Saturday's attack on Riyadh's airport, which killed 12 people and wounded over 300, according to aviation authorities.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," Guterres said in a statement.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called the attack a "dangerous escalation" and said the Iran-backed group must halt strikes on civilian targets.
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
"These murderous attacks at civilians must stop at once," she said, adding the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia".
Lightning offensive
Saturday's attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis, who captured swathes of Red Sea coastline in a lightning offensive last month.
The strike came in a week when the group intensified its attacks on the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport, where three people were also killed on Thursday, as well as other key targets in the world's largest crude oil exporter.
While the Houthis stopped short of claiming the strike, they threatened new attacks on the kingdom's airports, except for the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, warning passengers not to travel.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on social media platform X.
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed on Saturday, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
The US, Canadian, German, British and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport and the surrounding areas.
France's embassy earlier on Friday urged French nationals to take "utmost care" in Saudi Arabia because of "strikes in recent days by the Houthis". It also warned French citizens not to record images of zones that were hit, nor share any online.
On Sunday, France condemned the "heinous attack" by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis a day earlier on Riyadh's international airport and stressed "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
France, which is already lending troops and military equipment to Saudi Arabia, "will continue to remain by its side in its defence of its territory and its infrastructure", a foreign ministry statement said, calling on the Houthis to cease their attacks.
The French foreign ministry said a French woman was among those hurt.
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia on Sunday said staff working in the kingdom would now be required to request permission to use airports in the cities of Dammam and Jeddah, days after a similar order was issued for Riyadh.
'Appalling act of terror'
The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas denounced the attack as an "appalling act of terror".
"There can be no justification for indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure," she posted.
Kallas said she was in close contact with her Saudi counterpart and insisted enhancing cooperation between an EU naval mission in the Red Sea and a Riyadh-led maritime coalition was "vital".
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he "firmly condemns" the attack, which he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the attacks were "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation".
"What we've seen overnight is a dangerous escalation and I'm afraid an increasing pattern of behaviour from the Houthis that's targeting civilian sites in Saudi Arabia," he told Sky News.
"This is completely contemptible action and it's one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences, but also air-to-air refuelling," for Saudi jets to help the country defend itself against Houthi strikes, he said.
"We want to see an end to this conflict. It cannot be right that the Houthis are attacking civilian targets in this way," he added.
US President Donald Trump said the attack was "not acceptable" and that he was looking at joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in response.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," he told reporters at the White House.

articles.title: Trump tells Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy in Russia diesel deal spat
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump faces surging fuel prices ahead of midterm elections.
Trump, whose Republicans face dim prospects in next month's vote partly because of soaring energy costs, defended a deal allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets after saying Vladimir Putin strongly wanted to reach a settlement in Ukraine.
Trump accused Zelenskyy of blocking a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian refineries, while Kyiv and its European allies warned that easing pressure on Moscow would help fund the Kremlin's war.
Meanwhile, the latest Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including children.
Trump announced Friday that he had spoken to Putin and agreed Russia would release large amounts of diesel into global markets.
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay, with Zelenskyy telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision."
Asked about the criticism, Trump said Zelenskyy had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries and that the attacks risked worsening fuel shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Trump later said Putin was interested in ending the war.
"Russia would like to make a deal ... but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal," he told reporters.
"President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly."
The U.S. president also criticized Zelenskyy for not holding an election since Russia's 2022 invasion.
"I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Trump said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help sustain Russia's war effort.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy in a call.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion.
Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel.
"The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement.
Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order.
"The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote.
Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security.
FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest.
According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions.
Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses.
The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.
Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis.
His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9.
The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers.
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force.
A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts.
The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion.
The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025.
Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict.
Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict.
The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.

articles.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns - BBC
articles.summary: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns  BBC'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"  BBCUK's Healey can't risk a 'steady as you go' budget, think tank warns  ReutersIFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK spending pressures  The GuardianHealey Needs £35 Billion to Meet UK Spending Plans, IFS Says  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.
Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.
It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.
The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".
However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.
"But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."
He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".
However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.
The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.
"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.
"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.
"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.
The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.
These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.
The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.
Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.
'Breathing space'
Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.
However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.
But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.
However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.
The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.
That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.
The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.
But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.
It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.
However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.
