The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport.
Highlights
- Air defences intercept missile near airport, coalition says
- Houthis renew warnings against using Saudi airports
- Thirteen people killed in attack on airport on Saturday
- Riyadh airport remains closed on Sunday
- Conferences going ahead in Riyadh despite attacks, Saudi ministry says
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, as Saudi authorities reported people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. An unspecified number of people were injured, the Saudi civil aviation authority said, adding it was still assessing the damage.
The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport.
The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war in Yemen by the Yemeni government against the Iran-aligned group.
The airport has been closed since Saturday's attack. However, a long-planned international energy conference went ahead in Riyadh on Sunday as planned.
HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS
In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and also said the group had attacked the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco (2222.SE).
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation. Reuters has reached out to the Saudi media office and to Aramco for comment.
The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports.
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.
'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours, including the capital Sanaa and the group's stronghold Saada.
Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
INTERNATIONAL ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD
The five-day conference of international energy organizations WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport.
Meanwhile, a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available and it was not clear which ministers joined the meeting.
Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting the event, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.
German officials were trying to organise a return flight for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who was in Riyadh to attend the WPC conference and ministers' meeting.
She was supposed to return to Berlin on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely that her flight would not be able to take off due to the closure of the airport and alternatives were being considered.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes at all schools in Riyadh would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said. India's embassy in Riyadh said on Sunday one of its citizens injured in the attack had died, adding to the initial death toll of 12.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

articles.title: Oil chiefs pull out of Riyadh energy congress after airport missile strike - Financial Times
articles.summary: Oil chiefs pull out of Riyadh energy congress after airport missile strike  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Several senior international oil executives called off plans to attend an energy conference in Riyadh this week after a Houthi missile attack on the capital’s airport on Saturday that killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
Saudi Arabia said the strike — the third on King Khalid International Airport in a week — was a “cowardly terrorist attack” that would be met with a decisive response.
On Sunday, in a fourth attack on the airport killed one Pakistani resident and injured 11 other people, the civil aviation authority said.
As energy officials gathered at the ornate Ritz-Carlton Hotel on Sunday, a spokesperson for the Houthis issued renewed warnings to airlines, workers and passengers not to use Saudi airports or airspace. The airport in Riyadh remained closed on Sunday and the embassies of the US, Germany and other countries have advised their citizens to avoid it.
The Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh’s airport using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, as well as targeting Dammam airport and two Aramco oil sites in the Eastern Province. The group would “continue their operations deep inside Saudi”, Houthi military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Sare’e said.
The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP were all expected to attend the World Petroleum Council’s energy congress, which began on Sunday in Riyadh, but withdrew, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
“We made every effort to participate in WPC,” BP said. “Unfortunately, due to travel disruption, we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our longstanding partnerships across the region.” Shell declined to comment while Exxon and TotalEnergies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The kingdom’s flagship conference, the Future Investment Initiative, is also scheduled for this month. It typically attracts top executives from around the world. Saudi officials said both events would still take place.
Saturday’s attack is another reminder of how the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel in February has triggered retaliation by Tehran and its allies, spread violence across the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices.
“The repeated Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport and the heavy civilian toll carry, in my view, a deliberate message: raise the cost of Saudi decisions by threatening civilian lives, economic activity and confidence in the country’s security,” Maged al-Madhaji, co-founder of Sana’a Center, an independent Yemeni think-tank, wrote on social media platform X.
“The Houthis act with the audacity of a gambler who knows their opponent has much to protect,” he added.
The latest escalation comes after Yemen’s internationally recognised government, backed by Saudi Arabia, last week launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis.
The group in September took control of areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — which gives shipping access to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal — in a lightning offensive, giving the rebels the ability to monitor and attack Saudi ships and roiling global energy markets.
In the face of the Houthi threat, Saudi Arabia has been asking allies to provide defensive support. French President Emmanuel Macron said last month his country would send soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect Yanbu oil terminal on the Red Sea, which became a vital outlet for crude exports after the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Nato member Turkey last week said they had triggered a mutual defence pact for the first time, which would aim to ensure the “rapid deployment” of Pakistani and Turkish “military forces and capabilities” to Saudi Arabia.
US President Donald Trump has so far been reluctant to join the Saudi campaign against the Houthis as American interceptor stockpiles remain depleted after months of war with Iran.
Asked whether the US would consider striking the Iran-backed rebels, he said on Saturday: “We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
He called the attack on Riyadh’s airport “a terrible thing” and said he was planning to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Trump also said that “we have communication with the Houthis”. The group previously said they would not attack the US.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi commentator familiar with Riyadh’s thinking, said the kingdom’s large area size and multiple facilities that need protection posed a challenge.
“There is critical infrastructure in the east, there’s the pipeline, there’s facilities in the west. Air defences are coming in from the Turks, from the French and others are considering it,” he said. “Of course it’s a worry, but this is war and it won’t get normalised but a thicker skin will be developed to accept this comes with war.”
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 in an attempt to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis took over the capital, Sana’a.
A 2022 truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had largely held even during the early months of the US-Israeli war with Iran. But the truce collapsed in July after the Houthis, under mounting economic pressure, declared a blockade on the kingdom’s Red Sea ports, attacking Saudi tankers and targeting its oil infrastructure.

articles.summary: Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria leading options for Abraham Accords expansion, CSA report assesses  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
The Council for a Secure America (CSA) has ranked Kuwait as the Middle Eastern country most likely to join the Abraham Accords, followed by Lebanon and Syria, as changing political and security conditions reshape prospects for normalization with Israel.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
CSA released its “Abraham Accords Expansion Opportunities: Middle East Analysis” report on October 8, assessing nine Muslim-majority countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel: Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Iraq, Yemen, and Iran.
More than 80% of Israelis surveyed by CSA in June 2026 support the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan in 2020.
CSA Executive Director Jennifer Sutton said recent events have “reinforced the need for America's continued engagement in the region.”
The rankings were based on expert analysis, primary and secondary sources, and CSA polling. Researchers examined domestic political power, government structures, public opinion, statements by political leaders, relations with Israel and the United States, regional alliances, economic and energy interests, and ongoing conflicts. CSA said the rankings measure both governments’ willingness and political ability to normalize relations and could change as regional conditions evolve.
Kuwait thought to be closest to normalization with Israel, CSA survey shows
Kuwait ranked first despite its longstanding opposition to normalization and laws barring trade with Israel. CSA pointed to
Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah’s growing authority since suspending parliament in May 2024, closer ties with the UAE, and strong security ties with Washington. Kuwait also came under Iranian attack during the 2026 Iran War. Israel’s ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, said in September that Kuwait could join the accords within six months. 
Lebanon placed second following significant diplomatic activity with Israel. The countries signed a US-brokered “Trilateral Framework” in June under which Lebanon recognized Israeli sovereignty for the first time, followed by additional talks. CSA polling found 41% of Lebanese believed peace with Israel was likely, although only 32% supported normalization. Hezbollah’s continued presence and failure to fully disarm remain major obstacles.
Syria ranked third after talks with Israel accelerated following the fall of the Assad regime. President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in September that the countries had “almost reached agreements on 90%” of their outstanding issues, with a security agreement potentially preceding peace negotiations. CSA found 54% of Syrians believed peace was likely, 53% supported a security arrangement and 46% supported normalization. The dispute over the Golan Heights remains a key obstacle.
Saudi Arabia, previously seen as a leading candidate for normalization, has moved further away since October 7, 2023, and the 2026 Iran War. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in November 2025 that he was prepared to work toward joining the accords, but CSA said the Iran war and concerns over Israel’s regional alliances have made Riyadh increasingly wary.
Oman has also become less likely to normalize despite a history of contacts with Israel. Sultan Qaboos bin Said hosted several Israeli leaders, but under Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Oman has repeatedly rejected normalization and strengthened its role as a mediator with Iran and other regional actors.
Full normalization with Qatar dependent on peace agreement with Palestinians
Qatar maintains working contacts with Israel and serves as a mediator between Israel and Hamas, but says full diplomatic relations depend on an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement. CSA said Doha’s ties with Iran and support for the Muslim Brotherhood make accession to the accords unlikely in the near term.
Iraq remains an unlikely candidate because of Iranian influence and a 2022 law criminalizing normalization with Israel. CSA singled out Iraqi Kurdistan as an exception, citing its longstanding contacts with Israel and greater public openness toward diplomatic relations.
Yemen’s continuing civil war makes normalization highly unlikely. The Iran-backed Houthis are actively hostile to Israel, while other Yemeni factions have previously expressed openness to relations. CSA said a future postwar government could reconsider the issue, but little movement is possible while the country remains divided.
Iran ranked last. Relations with Israel ended after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and decades of hostility have developed into direct warfare. CSA concluded that normalization is not possible under Iran’s current regime.

articles.full_text:
As Israel prepared to assassinate Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his senior defense officials disagreed over whether to notify the Biden administration ahead of the operation, fearing Washington could try to stop the mission, according to Wall Street Journal editorial writer Elliot Kaufman and a second source familiar with the deliberations.
"140%, they won't approve of the mission," Netanyahu told senior Israeli defense officials, according to Kaufman, co-author of "In the War Room: The Inside Story of Israel's Fight Against Hamas and the Iranian Axis," who recounted the exchange in an interview with Fox News Digital.
Then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and IDF Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi favored informing Washington, believing the Americans might support a strike against a Hezbollah leader linked to the deaths of U.S. service members, according to Kaufman. Netanyahu, however, warned that then-U.S. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan would "jump out of his skin" if he learned of the plans.
The disagreement reflected a widening divide between Jerusalem and Washington over Israel's military campaign against Iran's regional proxies, as the Biden administration sought to prevent the fighting from escalating into a broader regional war.
Hezbollah: Netanyahu's warning about Washington
When Israeli jets struck Hezbollah's headquarters in Beirut on September 27, 2024, the Pentagon said it had received no advance warning. Gallant spoke with then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin while the operation was already underway.
The strike killed Nasrallah, who had led the Iranian-backed terrorist organization for more than three decades, marking a major turning point in Israel's campaign against Hezbollah, which opened a second front against Israel on October 8, 2023, a day after Hamas' deadly attack in southern Israel, and had since launched repeated rocket and missile attacks on northern Israeli communities.
Kaufman argued that Israel had spent nearly a year waiting for American diplomacy to end Hezbollah's attacks on its northern communities, without success.
"From Israel's point of view, it had been sitting and waiting for 10, 11 months while Hezbollah had been pounding the north of Israel with rockets and with anti-tank missiles, waiting for American diplomacy to succeed," he said. "It didn't work. Something had to change on the northern front."
Kaufman said the confrontation exposed a fundamental difference in how the two governments approached the war.
"The United States may not have been in Israel's war room, but it could never be denied a seat at the table when it asked," he said.
"What I was told from the Israeli prime minister's office is ‘America's goal is to de-escalate the war. Our goal is to win the war,' and we saw that clash at every point, especially during the Biden administration."
October 7: Netanyahu's reluctance and the question of accountability
The book, written by Kaufman and Jerusalem Post senior military analyst Yonah Jeremy Bob, also describes how Netanyahu initially resisted launching a full-scale ground invasion of Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, only to emerge later as one of the strongest advocates for continuing the war.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu had just seen the IDF, Israel's military, fail miserably on Oct. 7, and Israel's intelligence services fail miserably on October 7," Kaufman told Fox News Digital.
Senior American generals dispatched by President Biden also warned Israeli leaders that a ground invasion could end in military defeat, even in Gaza City, according to Kaufman.
Netanyahu eventually approved the ground operation on Oct. 27, 2023, after weeks of internal debate.
"Over time, he would gain confidence in the IDF, regain confidence in the military, in Israel's intelligence services, and end up outlasting, exhausting, or simply firing all of his war room rivals," Kaufman said.
Kaufman was more critical when asked about Netanyahu's accountability for Oct. 7.
"I have spoken to Prime Minister Netanyahu several times in person, even more on the phone. I had a three hour conversation with him extending well past midnight in Israel," Kaufman said. "I have not heard him take responsibility for what happened on October 7th."
Instead, Kaufman said, Netanyahu consistently points to the failure of senior military officials to alert him before the Hamas assault began. "What he says is, 6:29. They didn't wake me up until 6:29 in the morning on the day of October 7th," Kaufman recounted.
Those remarks came as a new controversy erupted in Israel over the official record of Netanyahu's actions on the morning of the attack.
In a lengthy interview broadcast Thursday by Israel's Channel 12, retired Maj. Gen. Avi Gil, who served as Netanyahu's military secretary at the time, said that the prime minister's chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, attempted to alter the official record of a telephone call between Gil and Netanyahu.
Gil said a stenographer told him she had been instructed to change the recorded time of their first secure telephone conversation from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. Gil said he had raised concerns about irregular recordkeeping with the attorney general's office in real time. Braverman has acknowledged seeking to change the recorded time but denied wrongdoing.
Gil also challenged the completeness of Netanyahu's public account of the events preceding the massacre, saying there were significant gaps between what occurred and what had been presented to the Israeli public and in his written statements.
The Likud party dismissed the alleged attempt to falsify the record, saying "the matter had been investigated by police two years earlier and that police had recommended closing the case because it lacked substance." However, prosecutors have not announced a decision to close the case.
Gil also said that opportunities to secure hostage agreements earlier in the war had been lost because of political considerations.
Asked by Channel 12 whether some hostages who died in captivity could have been brought home alive, Gil replied, "We could have."
He indicated that opposition to ceasefires and hostage deals from far-right ministers in Netanyahu's coalition influenced the prime minister's decisions.
While acknowledging that senior Israeli military officials believed Netanyahu was prolonging the war for political reasons, Kaufman challenged the argument that political survival was his sole motivation, pointing to Israel's subsequent campaigns against Hezbollah and Iran. "There were real strategic interests to be pursued," he said.
"Almost all of the real achievements of this war came later in the war," he said, arguing that the subsequent weakening of Hezbollah, the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria and the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities complicated claims that continued fighting served only Netanyahu's political interests.
Iran: How Israel helped convince Trump to strike
The book also examines how Israel's early military successes against Iran helped persuade President Donald Trump to authorize U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities during the 12-day war in June 2025.
Kaufman described how a Trump administration official showed him a map of Israeli airstrikes that had opened a route toward Fordow, Iran's heavily fortified underground nuclear facility.
According to Kaufman, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir subsequently made the case directly to Vice President JD Vance that American forces had an extraordinary opportunity to strike.
"You have a straight shot to Iran's nuclear sites. You will never have a better opportunity than this," Kaufman said, recounting Zamir's message to Vance.
Kaufman said the Israeli military chief told Vance that Israeli aircraft were already operating over the area, but that the U.S. possessed the heavy bunker-busting bombs necessary for the Fordow mission.
He credited the vice president with helping secure Trump's final authorization for Operation Midnight Hammer.
"Vice President Vance played a critical role in ultimately securing American participation in the highly successful 12-day war," Kaufman said.
The account challenges the notion that Trump was reluctantly drawn into the conflict by Netanyahu, Kaufman argued, portraying the president instead as responding to an opportunity created by Israel's demonstrated military capabilities.
Jake Sullivan's response was not received by the deadline.

articles.full_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi is welcomed by Indonesian children in Jakarta as he holds talks with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at Merdeka Palace on October 11, 2026. (Egyptian Presidency)
CAIRO – 11 October 2026: President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto issued a 16-point statement following their talks in Jakarta, highlighting bilateral ties, calling for Gulf de-escalation, and reaffirming their support for an independent Palestinian state.
Political Cooperation: The joint statement reaffirmed that two countries are committed to further enhancing political cooperation and coordination and have agreed on their Plan of Action for the Strategic Partnership.
Defense Cooperation: The two presidents agreed to deepen and expand the scope of the steadily growing defense and security cooperation between the two countries, further strengthening their respective national capabilities.
Bolstering Trade: The two presidents affirmed their commitment to deepening bilateral trade and economic cooperation by leveraging the vast potential and opportunities available to both sides.
They agreed on expanding market access, facilitating business and investment engagement, enhancing the effectiveness of the Joint Trade Committee, and advancing joint manufacturing projects in priority sectors.
Strategic Cooperation: The two leaders welcomed the tangible progress made in advancing strategic cooperation between Indonesia's "Danantara" and Egypt's "Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development" agency.
This reflects the two countries’ shared commitment to bolstering bilateral economic and investment relations, the statement added.
They emphasized the promising opportunities for cooperation in the production and distribution of crude palm oil and its derivatives, as well as phosphate fertilizers and related raw materials, thereby encouraging mutually beneficial investments and enhancing trade exchanges between the two countries.
Furthermore, the two presidents encouraged both entities to build upon the agreements reached, advance joint investment opportunities, and expand cooperation to encompass other strategic sectors, including infrastructure, energy, logistics, and agribusiness.
People-to-People Relations: The two presidents agreed to enhance people-to-people relations by broadening cooperation in education, culture, language, and youth engagement.
This includes expanding academic and institutional partnerships, student and school exchange programs, and launching a new partnership for capacity building and technical cooperation.
This would be achieved through the establishment of a framework for mutually agreed programs, enabling both countries to leverage their joint capabilities and achieve advanced development goals, the statement added.
Nile River, Water Scarcity: The two presidents acknowledged the growing challenges posed by climate change and water scarcity, as well as their repercussions for water and food security, sustainable development, and regional stability.
In this context, the Indonesian side took note of the vital importance of Nile water security for Egypt.
Both sides emphasized the importance of full adherence to the principles of international law governing transboundary watercourses, including the principle of not causing harm.
Israeli Violence, Settlement Activities: The two presidents expressed grave concern over continued violence and Israeli military operations across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, encompassing the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
They also condemned Israel’s illegal settlement policies and activities and called for their immediate and complete cessation, in accordance with the provisions of international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.
Palestinian Statehood: The two presidents reiterated their unwavering support for the establishment of an independent, sovereign, viable, and geographically contiguous State of Palestine, along the borders of June 4, 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital, based on the two-state solution, international law, and relevant United Nations resolutions.
Rejecting Displacement, Delivering Aid: They reaffirmed their categorical rejection of any attempts aimed at the forced displacement or expulsion of Palestinians from their homeland under any pretext.
They also reiterated their commitment to achieving a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace, including through the full implementation of President Trump’s comprehensive plan to end the conflict in Gaza.
The Indonesian side expressed its appreciation for Egypt’s pivotal role in facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip, affirming its commitment to continue providing humanitarian support to the Palestinian people.
Gulf De-escalation: Regarding the situation in the Gulf region, the two presidents expressed deep concern over the continued escalation and the expanding hostilities, resulting in serious repercussions for regional security and stability, the safety of civilians, freedom of navigation, energy security, and the global economy.
They called for immediate de-escalation and for all parties to exercise the utmost restraint.
They also emphasized the importance of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, adhering to international law and the UN Charter, and resolving conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy.
Indonesian Language Learning: Prabowo welcomed the decision issued by Al-Azhar University in November 2025 to include the Indonesian language within the curriculum of the Faculty of Languages and Translation.
Meanwhile, he encouraged the continued enhancement of cooperation in Arabic language education in Indonesia.
Ensuring Citizens’ Safety: El-Sisi and Prabowo underscored the importance of ensuring the safety and well-being of the citizens of both countries.
They encouraged enhanced cooperation between the competent authorities on consular matters and the provision of necessary assistance, in accordance with applicable national laws and regulations.
Strategic Alignment: In light of the rapid geopolitical and global challenges, the two presidents emphasized the importance of achieving greater strategic alignment and close coordination between Indonesia and Egypt in multilateral and regional forums.
The Egyptian president arrived in Jakarta on Saturday for an official visit to Indonesia, the final stop on his Asian tour, which also included South Korea and Malaysia.

articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia has returned to war in Yemen - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: Why Saudi Arabia has returned to war in Yemen  Responsible Statecraft
articles.full_text:
When Ansar Allah—commonly referred to as the Houthis—seized Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on September 10, 2026, they appeared to gain the upper hand in Yemen’s long-running conflict. However, in early October Saudi-backed government forces began to retake some of the captured territory and Saudi Arabia launched a punishing assault on Houthi positions from the air. France, Pakistan, and the United States have all sent personnel to help the kingdom counter the Houthi offensive.
Outside the region, some have portrayed the Houthi offensive as another theater within the broader US-Israeli war on Iran. However, this broader regional war is separate from the war in Yemen, which can be traced back to the Houthi takeover of Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014 and the decision by neighboring Saudi Arabia to launch a coalition to oust them in March 2015.
While the Houthis are certainly allied with Iran and benefit from the weapons and support that Tehran has covertly provided them since at least 2009, they have their own agenda: to consolidate their control over Yemen. They would pursue this political objective even if Washington and Tehran somehow agreed to end the war that Trump rashly launched. Still, their recent decision to escalate does reflect the sense of momentum produced by Iran’s success in withstanding American and Israeli attacks. Thus, even as these two conflicts are distinct, the Iran war is both exacerbating and heightening the effects of the violence in Yemen.
The Houthis’ Red Sea offensive
The catalyst for the latest round of violence came on July 13, 2026, when an Iranian civilian plane—carrying a Houthi delegation that had attended the funeral of Iran’s assassinated Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei—returned to Yemen. When the plane attempted to land at Sanaa International Airport, the runway was bombed. Yemen’s internationally recognized government—under the leadership of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC)—took responsibility for the attack, while the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which supports the PLC. As a result of the attack, the plane was forced to land in Houthi-controlled Hodeidah. On July 20, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait in retaliation for its attacks and ongoing restrictions on Houthi-controlled territory. The Houthis subsequently targeted Saudi petroleum facilities and oil tankers in the Red Sea.
The attack on Sanaa Airport officially ended the truce that had largely held between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since April 2022.
The attack on Sanaa Airport officially ended the truce that had largely held between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since April 2022. Even before this incident, however, the Houthis appeared to have already been preparing for a return to conflict, mobilizing their fighters and moving materiel into position. In a June 16, 2026, speech, the Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi announced that the group was ready for combat and called for official and grassroots action to end what he described as more than 11 years of Saudi aggression and blockade.
The speech shifted the Houthis’ narrative away from their support for Palestinians, which had become central to the group’s domestic legitimacy in the context of Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza since October 7, 2023. In subsequent months, as the Houthis began striking Israeli ships in the Red Sea in retaliation for their violence against Palestinians, their credibility at home substantially increased, helping paper over their repression and failure to improve the daily lives of Yemenis under their control. The Houthis’ support for Palestine also drove recruitment and raised their international profile. Yet the group also paid for its solidarity with Palestinians, with the United States and Israel hitting Houthi areas with deadly air strikes. In August 2025, Israel assassinated several Houthi cabinet ministers, including the prime minister. Following Netanyahu’s stated commitment to a ceasefire in Gaza in October 2025, the Houthis signaled a pause in their campaign against Israel. Despite Israel’s daily violations of said ceasefire, the Houthis have limited their attacks on Israel, an indication that the group may wish to avoid returning to open conflict with Tel Aviv. Instead, the Houthis shifted focus to Riyadh’s restrictions on their airspace and seaports, as well as Saudi support for the various competing groups that oppose Houthi rule.

The Houthi resurgence
Over the past four years, the Houthis have improved their military capabilities. Increasingly, they can manufacture weapons inside Yemen, although a network of providers, including Iran, continues to provide the raw materials and other components they need. Analysts have claimed that the Houthis have been bringing in large shipments of military material, equipment, and weapons. There are also reports that they have used Claude, Anthropic’s AI tool, to develop guided weapons. As early as 2017, the Houthis experimented with the use of a drone boat, and in the years since have remained at the cutting edge in terms of their use of emerging technologies to threaten adversaries with far more resources and firepower.
The Houthis’ ability to swiftly seize the Red Sea coast from forces loyal to the PLC was further facilitated by the withdrawal of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from Yemen in January 2026 under pressure from Saudi Arabia. Until early 2026, the UAE provided significant assistance to Yemen’s southern secessionist movement, led by the Southern Transitional Council (STC). The chairman of the STC, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, was also a member of the PLC. However, in December 2025, STC forces suddenly took large swathes of territory in eastern Yemen, which included areas along the Saudi border in the provinces of Hadramawt and al-Mahra. Saudi Arabia responded quickly, bombing Emirati ships transporting weapons to the STC and insisting that the UAE fully withdraw from Yemen. Under Saudi pressure, the STC leadership announced the dissolution of the group, while al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE. The PLC rescinded al-Zubaidi’s membership of the council along with another STC ally, the former governor of Hadramawt, replacing them with two new figures. Yet Saudi Arabia’s attempt to quash the STC hardly quelled demands for southern independence. Instead, it appeared to alienate separatists who previously supported the PLC in the hopes that by doing so, it would lead to an independent southern Yemen.
The PLC’s initial inability to repel the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast in the current conflict—even with Saudi backing—was seen as a sign of the ruling government’s overall ineffectiveness.
The PLC, in turn, owes much of its own rise to power to Saudi Arabia. After the Arab Spring protests forced President Ali Abdullah Saleh to step down and end his more than 33-year rule over Yemen in 2012, Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi led the internationally recognized government that replaced him, initially with Saudi support. What was meant to be a two-year interim position for Hadi, however, turned into ten. His rule finally ended when Saudi Arabia withdrew its backing and transferred authority to the PLC. The PLC initially comprised eight men, four aligned primarily with Saudi Arabia and four with the UAE.
These dynamics created deep internal divisions in the PLC, which has also been accused of corruption and an inability to improve the quality of life for the population under its authority. Some Yemeni critics have called for reforms to make the PLC more accountable and representative of all Yemenis. In response to such criticisms, in January 2025, PLC chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced a crackdown on corruption. Nevertheless, the PLC’s initial inability to repel the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast in the current conflict—even with Saudi backing—was seen as a sign of the ruling government’s overall ineffectiveness.
Riyadh and the Houthis: What do they want?
Over the course of the Houthis’ war with Saudi-backed forces from 2015 until 2022, the group advanced its military capabilities, largely through covert Iranian support. The turning point in this war came in March 2022, when the Houthis hit Saudi Arabia during the Formula One Saudi Arabian Grand Prix in Jeddah. The attack showed the Houthis were capable of not only deterring tourists and investors from coming to Saudi Arabia but also threatening the success of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitious Vision 2030 plan to transform the kingdom’s economy and society. Only after the attack did Saudi Arabia agree to a two-month United Nations (UN)-brokered truce in April 2022.
By March 2023, Saudis were reportedly eager to find a longer-term agreement to end their costly and ultimately futile involvement in Yemen. Over the next few months, Riyadh engaged in direct talks with the Houthis, mediated by Oman, in pursuit of that goal, resulting in a broader UN-brokered roadmap agreement in December 2023. Under the terms of this agreement, Saudi Arabia would reportedly pay public sector salaries, including in Houthi-held territory, and would ease restrictions on air and seaports. The deal would have also enabled the resumption of oil exports and initiated an inclusive, Yemeni-led political settlement under UN auspices. In effect, the deal would have disempowered the PLC, which depends largely on Saudi support. When the Houthis initiated hostilities against Israel in late 2023—which prompted the US to launch Operation Prosperity Guardian against them in response—the Saudis were notably absent, unwilling to risk a resumption of transborder attacks.

articles.title: Year into cease-fire, promised peace never arrived for Gazans
articles.summary: A year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brough...
articles.full_text:
A year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace.
Israel has reduced its attack intensity but continues strikes and now controls over 70% of Gaza. The cease-fire plan's promised reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory has not materialized.
"Nothing has changed for the better; everything has got worse, they lie to us, it is all lies," Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, said.
"Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues and we cannot even find a moment's peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead."
On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance, blown-out windows gape from building facades still standing.
Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the cease-fire.
"We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats," the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerrycans of water back to his tent.
Israel's genocidal war, which broke out after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, has displaced almost all of Gaza's more than 2 million residents at least once.
With 82% of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, according to the U.N., many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where lack of hygiene has led to outbreaks of disease.
Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis, said he had yet to see the cease-fire take effect.
"It has been a full year since the cease-fire was declared, yet it exists only on paper," he said.
The agreement's second phase called for a political transition away from Hamas rule, with technocrat Ali Shaath appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Five countries, including Morocco, have agreed to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) tasked with post-war preparations, but its troops have not yet started operating in Gaza.
Israel controls all entry points into the territory and continues to allow only a limited amount of aid, keeping the price of basic goods too high for ordinary Gazans like Ismail Hamouda.
The 47-year-old father, displaced from Jabalia in the north to Gaza City, listed what residents still lack: potable water, food, financial assistance.
"Here in the displacement camps, we thought that after a year of cease-fire things would improve," he said. "Unfortunately, the situation is worsening gradually. We are still displaced."

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' leaders defy crackdown to continue protests
articles.summary: Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after their release from police custody, following a crackdown on demonstrations demanding the resignat...
articles.full_text:
Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after their release from police custody, following a crackdown on demonstrations demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over controversial voter list revisions.
The protests were triggered after authorities removed more than 130 million voters from the list since last year. Critics say the move is politically motivated. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny manipulation allegations.
The Cockroach Janata Party's three leaders – Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka – were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year,” Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests.
Police boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi.
After his release, Dipke called Modi "an embarrassment to India.”
"Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X.
Das, a spokesperson for the movement, urged supporters to take to the streets. "A situation has been created where the state is at war with its own citizens," he told reporters Sunday.
Following Saturday's protests, authorities launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers.
Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city.
Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said.
Small groups of protesters returned to the Indian capital Sunday, staging marches across the city. The police quickly broke up most of the demonstrations, detaining some protesters again.
Protesters are demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner. Modi’s party has said the voter revision is needed to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The Cockroach movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience.
Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

articles.title: UN reports 109 dead when migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
articles.summary: At least 15 children were among 109 migrants who died while 116 others went missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti on Oct. 8, a U.N. agency said Sunday. Survivors said...
articles.full_text:
At least 15 children were among 109 migrants who died while 116 others went missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti on Oct. 8, a U.N. agency said Sunday.
Survivors said the vessel, carrying 350 people from Djibouti to Yemen, capsized north of Obock, Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said in a statement.
“This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said in the statement.
He said IOM teams were on the ground alongside Djiboutian authorities to provide emergency aid.
Coissac added, “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.”
The statement said the 109 bodies recovered included 52 men, 42 women and 15 children (nine girls and six boys).
More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals.
“Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to make this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East,” the IOM said.
